newsitem.title: BELARUS: Lukashenko says West, East aim to smother Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Lukashenko says West, East aim to smother Belarus.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, facing chilly relations with Moscow and Washington over his authoritarian rule, accused critics from West to East of trying to smother his former Soviet republic of Belarus.

"They have started to suffocate us openly, to suffocate us in the West and unfortunately somewhat in the East, but we will soon remove the masks from a few people," he told the population of 10 million in a live broadcast on television and radio.
"We have no one left to count on," he said, referring to the economic situation in Belarus, where international lending bodies have suspended credits pending faster reforms.
The 42-year-old former farm boss made no direct comment on a row with Washington over the expulsion of a U.S. diplomat during the special three-hour programme on the spring sowing campaign.
Washington said it "deplored" the action, saying the diplomat was carrying out normal diplomatic duties by observing a rally and withdrew its ambassador for consultations.
Minsk had accused the expelled diplomat, first secretary Serzh Alexandrov, of "provocative" actions at a nationalist rally which erupted in clashes on Sunday.

Nor did Lukashenko refer directly to criticism by the Kremlin of his country's treatment of journalists working for the Russian media, though he said they were Belarussian citizens, implying it was an internal matter.

The Kremlin complained after Belarus withdrew the accreditation of Russian NTV channel's correspondent in Minsk and said it might deport him. Foreign journalists have been barred from the main television centre in Minsk since Sunday.

But Lukashenko, who swept to power on vows of closer ties with Russia to the east and is backed by most Belarussians, made digs at a string of countries which criticised him over a referendum last year in which he vastly increased powers.
"There are more than enough people who oppose us carrying out normal work -- not only in our country but beyond its borders," he said.
Lukashenko said he was concerned about the future actions of ethnic Poles living in western Belarus and asked the governor of Grodno region on the Polish border to keep an eye on them.
"Certain forces are trying to involve them in actions and organise centres in Poland, Lithuania and the Czech Republic.
"I cannot say everything openly now, but we will tell you what is happening. We will send a special group and pass on the information in a chain," he said.
He seemed to be hinting at activities by Zenon Poznyak and Sergei Naumchik, leaders of the opposition Belarussian Popular Front who were awarded political asylum in the United States last August.
He said Poznyak had visited Warsaw and left for Lithuania. Naumchik is reported to be in the Czech capital, Prague.

In a dig at Russia, Lukashenko congratulated technicians for organising the programme, during which officials talked to him from their offices on a special intercom system. "I congratulate you that our intercom meeting on the technical level exceeded Russia, with whom we are competing as you know," he said.
Lukashenko is opposed by a loose union of prominent politicians, nationalist and intellectuals mostly in Minsk.
Washington has recently cut of $40 million in aid to Belarus over its human rights record, accusing authorities of using force to break up protests and of arresting bystanders.
